items.heading: A Career After Library Science
items.text: A career after library science is not one job title. It is a small cluster of genuinely different work: physical and digital library operations, government-scale librarian posts reached through UGC-NET, and a growing corporate side, knowledge management, digital archiving, and information governance, that most first-year LIS students never hear about in an orientation talk.

items.heading: Library and Information Science Covers
items.text: Library and Information Science covers how information gets organised, catalogued, preserved, and retrieved, in physical libraries, digital archives, and, increasingly, corporate knowledge systems. It is a humanities-and-science field, not an engineering one, built around classification schemes, cataloguing standards, reference services, and, in its modern form, digital repository and database-management skills.

items.heading: Most Articles on This Topic
items.text: Most articles on this topic default to listing government and school librarian roles first because they are the most familiar. Ranked honestly by realistic pay ceiling and growth headroom instead, the order looks different: corporate knowledge management and digital archiving currently scale further than the traditional government route, because private employers pay for information systems that directly affect revenue, compliance, or research output, and those pay bands are not capped by a government pay matrix. The skill portfolio you build inside whichever track you pick, not the ranking itself, is what actually moves you toward higher income opportunities from here.

visuals.heading: Blis/mlis Entry Routes and Eligibility

rows: Bachelor of Library and Information Science (BLIS)

A 1-year professional degree open to graduates of any discipline (a Bachelor's degree in any subject is the eligibility, not a specific stream). Some universities also run a 3-year integrated BLIS after Class 12.
Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS)

1-2 years after a BLIS (or, at some universities, directly after any Bachelor's degree). This is the usual minimum qualification for librarian and information-officer posts, not just library-assistant roles.
UGC-NET for Library and Information Science

A national-level qualifying exam conducted by the NTA. Required for Assistant Professor (library science) posts and, at most universities, for university and college librarian posts specifically, alongside the MLIS.
Ph.D in Library and Information Science
Optional, but relevant for senior academic-library leadership roles and for anyone aiming at teaching library science itself at a university.
